capitalismdebates.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
capitalismdebates.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
capitalismdebates.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).
capitalismdebates.representative_figures_and_works: Transition: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb (1950); Takahashi (1952); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976). Brenner debate and political Marxism: Brenner (1976; 1977; 1982); Postan and Hatcher, Croot and Parker, Wunder, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Cooper (1978); Klíma (1979); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985); Wood (1981; 1991; 1999/2002; 2001); Harman (1989); Callinicos (1990). Industrialisation: Toynbee (1884, context); Mendels (1972); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977); Wrigley (1988); Berg and Hudson (1990/1992); Crafts and Harley (1992); de Vries (1994; 2008); Mokyr (2002; 2009); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023). Great Divergence: Wong (1997); Frank (1998); Landes (1998); Pomeranz (2000); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Huang (2002); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021). Slavery and capitalism: Williams (1944); Drescher (1977); Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987); Inikori (2002); Hall et al. (2014); Johnson (2013); Baptist (2014); Beckert (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds, 2016); Olmstead and Rhode (2017; 2018); Hilt (2017); Burnard and Riello (2020).
capitalismdebates.scope_note: A Debate entry with five components, each with its own strands: the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism. It gathers exchanges; the related field strands remain in place, while person entries hold the relationships stated below. The field strands, not moved, are: marx/transition, economic/marxist, economic/household_demand, economic/wrigley_growth, economic/regional_divergence, economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute (the Huang–Pomeranz exchange), economic/slavery_productivity_exchange, economic/empire, global/comparison, global/reciprocal_comparison_resources, global/protoindustry_trade_limits, consumption/household_labor, technology/invention_adoption, demography/aggregate_population, dependency/worldsystems, atlantic/earlier and quant/slavery_debate. Existing person entries (Dobb, Hilton, Williams, Pomeranz, Huang, Hall) keep their own relations; Brenner and Wood gained person entries in 1.145; Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong follow in 1.146. Readings are recorded per source, many through publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core chapter openings or reviewers; unread books are given only as named readers report them. Quotations from another copy of The Brenner Debate (1985) were withdrawn before drafting. The 'California School' is a readers' label, attributed by Frank (2001) and Vries (2009) to Goldstone. Toynbee (1884) is a dated precursor, not a start. Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong hold their contributions to the debate on their own entries (the arrows drawn for them in 1.145 from demography, consumption and technology now start from those entries); Allen and Beckert remain roster rows here.

representative_people.context: Defined feudalism by 'the relations between the direct producer and his overlord' and answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950, pp. 158, 160). Brenner acknowledged a 'great debt' to him (1977).
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy (1950)

representative_people.context: Feudalism as 'a system of production for use', dissolved by 'causes external to the system', chiefly trade (1950, pp. 136, 141), offered as a correction from within: 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct' (p. 142). Brenner (1977) traced Wallerstein's and Frank's 'neo-Smithian' Marxism back to him.
Developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour power, and pressed Dobb for fuller French and German comparison (1952, pp. 313–315).
Collected the transition debate (1976) and introduced the Brenner debate as 'a continuation' of it (1985, p. 1); 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978) traced the Marxist view from Dobb to Bois.
representative_people.works: The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (ed., 1976); "A Crisis of Feudalism" (1978); introduction to The Brenner Debate (1985)

representative_people.context: Class structure, not population or trade, decides the effects of demographic and commercial change (1976–82); a critique of 'neo-Smithian Marxism' (1977); with Isett, social-property relations against Pomeranz's coal and colonies (2002).
representative_people.works: Past and Present (1976; 1982); NLR (1977); with Isett, JAS (2002)

representative_people.context: The leading exponent of 'political Marxism', by others' accounts; the origin of capitalism in English agrarian social-property relations (1991–2002); answered that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside' (2002).
representative_people.works: NLR (1981); The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991); The Origin of Capitalism (1999/2002); "Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism" (2001)

representative_people.context: A Marxist who welcomed Brenner's attack on 'the Malthusian model' while 'radically disagreeing with his methodological orientation' (1978, p. 107); called the approach 'political Marxism' (pp. 115–116, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990).
With Hatcher, called Brenner's charges against the demographic historians 'groundless' (1978, p. 64).
Co-author with Postan of the 1978 reply to Brenner.
Defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model and found Brenner's argument 'extremely insular' (1978, pp. 101–102); Brenner had criticised his Languedoc cycle (1976).
With Parker, found Brenner's England–France contrast 'open to serious doubt' (1978, p. 79).
Co-author with Croot of the 1978 comparison of France and England.
Found Brenner's east–west German contrast had 'fallen victim to the Prussian myth' (1978, p. 91).
Sympathised with Brenner against demographic determinism and placed him in 'a long line of expositors beginning with the Physiocrats' (1978, p. 138).
Bohemia as 'a variant case' in Brenner's comparison (1979, p. 192).
Co-editor of The Brenner Debate (1985).
Co-editor of The Brenner Debate (1985).

In his own account (1974, read in part), a world-economy's division of labour defines the unit of analysis, with external arenas distinguished from internal exchange, and coerced labour can belong to capitalism. Brenner's 1977 critique treated the world-system as an outgrowth of Sweezy's position.

Target of Brenner's 1977 critique, credited with breaking stage theory; ReOrient (1998) put Asia at the centre of the early modern world economy, was announced to debate Landes (December 1998) and reviewed Pomeranz as 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution' (2001).
representative_people.works: Development of underdevelopment (1966–); ReOrient (1998); JAS review (2001)

representative_people.context: Called Wood's political Marxism 'little more than a sociology of domination' while finding Brenner's 1977 critique 'a valuable corrective' (1990).
Brenner 'take[s] up Dobb's argument, but simplif[ies] it' (1989); debated Brenner in London (2004).
Criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal, drawing on Blaut (2001).
His posthumous lectures defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations' and found that it produced 'wealth without producing well-being' (1884).
representative_people.works: Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884)

representative_people.context: With Harley, revised British output growth downward while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992, abstract); his 1985 book is known here through Berg and Hudson.
representative_people.works: British Economic Growth during the Industrial Revolution (1985, unread); with Harley (1992)

representative_people.context: Co-author of the 1992 restatement; reviewing Mokyr (2010), doubted whether 'causation from Enlightenment … actually existed'.
With Hudson, argued that growth accounting 'mis-specified' the Industrial Revolution and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992).
Co-author with Berg of the 1992 rehabilitation of the Industrial Revolution.

Questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime (1988; 2013; 2016). Berg and Hudson criticised the aggregative demography he built with Schofield (1990).
representative_people.works: Continuity, Chance and Change (1988); "Energy and the English Industrial Revolution" (2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016)

representative_people.context: Named market-oriented rural industry 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper' (1972) and later 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); Stone credited him, 'so far as I can discover', as 'the originator of the word and idea of proto-industrialization'.
With Medick and Schlumbohm, rural industry 'in the genesis of capitalism' (1977; English 1981). Contents read only.
Göttingen collaborator on the proto-industrial family economy (1976), chapter 2 of the 1977 book. Body unread.
Third Göttingen co-author of Industrialisierung vor der Industrialisierung (1977).

Proposed the 'industrious revolution' as a household-level, demand-side change preceding the supply-side Industrial Revolution, in response to the Crafts–Harley revision (1994); Pomeranz used it for Chinese households (2000). Van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009) found consumption made 'a new deus ex machina'.

The 'Industrial Enlightenment' as 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002); against Pomeranz, coal and ghost acreage are 'not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job' (2002); found Parthasarathi's case 'simply unpersuasive' (2012). With Kelly and Ó Gráda, labour quality and mechanical skills (2014; 2023).
representative_people.works: conference draft (October 2002); The Enlightened Economy (2009); EH.Net review (2012); with Kelly and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Max Weber Lecture (2007)

representative_people.context: 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap': the Industrial Revolution 'was invented in Britain … because it paid to invent it there' (2009); answered Humphries with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract); with colleagues, disputed Yangzi–England wage parity (2011).
representative_people.works: The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009); EHR (2011; 2015)

representative_people.context: Charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' that 'focuses on men and male wages', proposing cheap female and child labour instead (2013, abstract).

Compared Chinese and European trajectories without treating Europe as the norm (1997); Pomeranz followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed', with 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures'. With Rosenthal, explained divergence by political scale and war (2011), as Ma's review reports; Ma found the evidence 'fairly meager'.
representative_people.works: China Transformed (1997); with Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence (2011); “Divergence Displaced” (2016)

representative_people.context: The Great Divergence (2000) set the debate's later terms. His critics are drawn on several distinct arrows: named critics from this entry (wages, the state, regional accounts), Brenner and Isett from Brenner's entry, Mokyr from his own entry, and Huang on his own. Vries (2013, p. 17) reports Pomeranz's 2011 reassessment that parity had probably gone by 1750 'if not in 1700', drawn as his contribution to this entry.
representative_people.works: The Great Divergence (2000); replies to Huang (2002; 2003); 'Ten Years After' (2011, unread; reported by Vries)

representative_people.context: Named the 'California School', according to Frank (2001) and Vries (2009); argued for pre-modern 'efflorescences' while locating the breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture (2002, abstract).
representative_people.works: "Efflorescences and Economic Growth in World History" (2002)

representative_people.context: The Eurocentric counterpoint as named readers describe him: a debate notice written from Frank's side (1998) and Frank (2001) make culture, values and institutions his explanation of the West's lead; Vries (2013), who counts him among the Eurocentrists, notes that none of them 'ever writes in terms of "inevitability"'. His first chapter, the only part read, argues from geography and does not by itself verify that account.
representative_people.works: The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998)

representative_people.context: Carried the 'California hypothesis' to India (Mokyr 2012): British divergence came from Indian cotton competition and wood shortage with state policy, not European difference; rejects Brenner's English exceptionalism (2011, pp. 2–5).
representative_people.works: Why Europe Grew Rich and Asia Did Not (2011)

representative_people.context: With Wong, political fragmentation and war in Europe against unity in China, and the urban location of manufacturing (2011), as Ma's review reports. Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence' and the evidence on Chinese public goods 'even shakier'; the book is unread.

Admired The Great Divergence but found differences, not 'surprising resemblances', in agriculture and the state; Californians 'would be well-advised to broaden their approach' (2009); surveys the school and its critics (2013).
With Gupta (2006) and with Guan and Li (2021), wages and national accounts date the divergence before 1800, around 1700 in the latter.
His exchange with Pomeranz over involution and coal (2002–2003) is drawn on its own arrows and held in economic's dispute strands.
Co-author with Brenner of the 2002 property-relations critique of Pomeranz.

Capitalism and Slavery (1944) set the agenda; Burnard and Riello (2020) treat four of its arguments as the new history of capitalism's inheritance, and its industrialisation claim as the most contested.
Contested Williams's decline explanation of abolition (1977); writes of 'the Williams-Drescher debate' (1997).
representative_people.works: Econocide (1977); "Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years" (1997)

representative_people.context: Co-edited the 1987 volume on Williams's legacy; judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello).
representative_people.works: British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (ed. with Engerman, 1987)

representative_people.context: Co-edited the 1987 volume; with Eltis, judged the growth linkages of slavery and the slave trade to British industry 'not particularly large' (2000, as Hilt reports).
representative_people.works: British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); with Eltis, JEH (2000)

representative_people.context: Atlantic trade and Africans as producers and consumers made the Industrial Revolution (2002, as O'Rourke reports); 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis' (Hilt 2017).
representative_people.works: Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002)

representative_people.context: With the UCL Legacies of British Slave-ownership team, investigated slave-ownership's British legacies through the compensation records of the 1830s: the jointly written introduction finds them 'entirely supportive of Williams' on slave-derived wealth, qualifies his 'decline' thesis and says of the industrialisation controversy 'Our material cannot resolve these controversies' (2014). She sets 'a modified version of Williams's thesis' among economic historians, naming Pomeranz and Inikori (2014). Her edges to Williams and economic history stay as drawn in revision 1.144.
representative_people.works: Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014, with Draper, McClelland, Donington and Lang)

representative_people.context: 'I call this system war capitalism': slavery, expropriation and armed trade as the foundation of industrial capitalism (2014); an early definer of the history of capitalism (Hilt 2017).
representative_people.works: Empire of Cotton (2014); with Rockman, Slavery’s Capitalism (2016)

representative_people.context: Argued that 'systematized torture' drove cotton productivity and the Industrial Revolution (as Hilt quotes him); The Economist withdrew its review of the book and apologised (2014). Book unread.
representative_people.works: The Half Has Never Been Told (2014)

representative_people.context: An 'ethnography of the Cotton South' (Hilt), who does not count himself a historian of capitalism (Hilt). Book unread.

With Rhode, found that Johnson, Beckert and Baptist 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017, AHA programme abstract); they attribute the observed increase in cotton-picking productivity primarily to biological innovation (as Hilt reports their work).
Co-author with Olmstead of the 2017 paper and 2018 article.

Surveyed ten books of the history of capitalism: 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine these books' effectiveness as social criticism' (2017). He granted that economic research 'casts doubt on some of these arguments and lends support to others', and called for 'dialogue, if not collaboration'.
With Riello, from Atlantic and global history: coercion overstated, US cotton 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution', consumption neglected (2020).
Co-author with Burnard of the 2020 critique of the new history of capitalism.

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
strands.works: Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013); Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Beckert, Empire of Cotton (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds), Slavery’s Capitalism (2016); Olmstead and Rhode (AHA 2017; EEH 2018); Hilt (JEH 2017); Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020); Regele (2023)

coverage.basis: Surveyed through 2000 in the research of 2026-10-18 (data/extension-2026/capitalism-debate-2026-10-18/evidence-industrialisation.md, evidence-great-divergence.md, evidence-slavery-capitalism.md; data/extension-2026/brenner-2026-10-18/evidence-brenner.md, evidence-transition-political-marxism.md). Selected later interventions are dated individually through 2023 (Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda; Regele). Later work, including substantial later political Marxism and Great Divergence literature, is not yet surveyed for this entry.
